title: Kabul’s classrooms, rebuilt in the Taliban’s own image
gist: Registered madrassas in Afghanistan have grown from around 5,000 before August 2021 to more than 23,000 today, enrolling over 3.65 million children, as public schools, universities and teacher-training colleges are converted into religious institutions with rewritten curricula. The author argues that international diplomacy fixated on reopening girls' schools has missed a sweeping ideological re-engineering project that would leave classrooms unrecognisable even if the ban were lifted tomorrow — and that engagement-breeds-moderation has been falsified.

insights.claim: Registered madrassas in Afghanistan have risen from around 5,000 before the republic's fall in August 2021 to more than 23,000 today, enrolling more than 3.65 million children, according to the exiled Afghan civil society organisation the Hamrah Network.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A 4.6x expansion in five years quantifies an institutional transformation that will shape Afghan human capital and security risk for a generation — the base rate for any 'normalisation' scenario.
insights.quote: the number of registered madrassas has risen from around 5,000, to more than 23,000 today, enrolling more than 3.65 million children

insights.claim: Public schools, universities, teaching colleges and other public facilities in Afghanistan have been repurposed as religious institutions, meaning the physical and institutional base for secular education has been dismantled, not merely paused.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Reconstruction of secular education would require rebuilding infrastructure and staff, not a policy reversal — reset the cost and timeline of any future aid program.
insights.quote: Public schools, universities and teaching colleges, and other public facilities have been repurposed as religious institutions.
insights.locator: Girls shut out of secondary education

insights.claim: The madrassa system extends into non-conventional settings, with 92 madrassas inside prisons and around 9,000 orphans receiving religious education.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Prison and orphanage penetration signals a recruitment pipeline into the most vulnerable populations — a specific indicator for terrorism-risk analysts.
insights.quote: The report says there are 92 madrassas inside prisons, and around 9,000 orphans receiving religious education.
insights.locator: The reach of this project extends well beyond conventional schools

insights.claim: Girls shut out of secondary education are being channelled into female madrassas as their only educational option, meaning the girls' education ban has not created an educational vacuum but a redirected ideological one.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: The policy debate framed as 'girls out of school' understates the problem: girls are in school, in a different curriculum.
insights.quote: Girls shut out of secondary education are channelled into female madrassas as their only educational option.
insights.locator: Girls shut out of secondary education

insights.claim: The Afghan madrassa curriculum emphasises Koranic memorisation, Hadith studies and conservative Hanafi jurisprudence alongside Taliban-approved political instruction, with some madrassas using a text titled Lessons of Jihad.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Curriculum content, not enrolment numbers, is where militarisation risk sits — a concrete artefact for monitoring bodies to track.
insights.quote: Some madrassas use a text titled Lessons of Jihad, the report says, while some Taliban figures have publicly called for religious schools to instil jihadi and military concepts.

insights.claim: Madrassa graduates are increasingly recruited into the Taliban's religious, judicial and security institutions, making the education system a direct staffing pipeline for the state.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Locks in ideological continuity of Afghan officialdom for decades — any bet on internal liberalisation of the bureaucracy is misplaced.
insights.quote: Graduates are increasingly recruited into the Taliban’s religious, judicial and security institutions.

insights.claim: The system teaches children that loyalty to the regime outranks loyalty to family, with some parents withdrawing sons after discovering they were being encouraged to monitor and report on relatives — an extension of ideological control into the household.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Household-level surveillance suppresses civil society formation, closing off the usual channels through which external actors build local partners.
insights.quote: “Be aware that we now have informants in each one of your households.”
insights.locator: It quotes an official of Taliban intelligence

insights.claim: The subjugation of women and the remaking of education are complementary, not separate, policies — one excludes women from public and intellectual life while the other bends the beliefs of the next generation.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A framework that reframes conditionality: negotiating on the girls' ban alone addresses half of a single integrated program.
insights.quote: The subjugation of women and the remaking of education are complementary policies – one excluding women from public and intellectual life, the other seeking to bend the beliefs and behaviour of the next generation.
insights.locator: The subjugation of women and the remaking

insights.claim: Reopening girls' schools tomorrow would come too late, because many classrooms would offer little of the modern education that existed before 2021 — the benchmark diplomats have set as the condition for recognition has been quietly hollowed out.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Warns that the headline diplomatic win most governments are waiting for would be substantively empty — do not treat a reopening announcement as evidence of change.
insights.quote: Even if the ban was lifted tomorrow, many classrooms would offer little of the modern education that existed before 2021.

insights.claim: International engagement with the Taliban is steadily increasing — diplomats citing pragmatism, aid agencies humanitarian imperatives, investors opportunity — even as the regime undertakes one of the world's most sweeping projects of ideological re-engineering.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Flags a widening gap between de-facto normalisation trends and on-the-ground trajectory — relevant reputational and political risk for investors entering Afghanistan.
insights.quote: Diplomats talk of pragmatism, aid agencies of humanitarian imperatives, investors of opportunity, and apologists of normalcy.

insights.claim: The long-standing diplomatic premise that governing is harder than fighting and would therefore push the Taliban toward moderation is contradicted by the evidence — the madrassa expansion is the clearest demonstration of the movement's actual vision, not an aberration.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Directly falsifies the theory of change underlying most Western engagement policy — a reason to expect engagement without behavioural convergence.
insights.quote: the expansion of the madrassa system is not an aberration but the “clearest demonstration of the Taliban’s actual vision”
insights.locator: For years, diplomats have justified engagement

insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Institutional absorption without doctrinal renunciation means the capability persists inside the state — a live consideration for regional security risk pricing.

insights.claim: The Taliban project is more radical and deliberately retrograde than authoritarian models such as China's or Iran's, which maintain substantial technical and scientific sectors alongside political and ideological control.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A useful taxonomy: authoritarianism that preserves technical capacity can still generate growth; this variant forecloses it, capping Afghanistan's long-run economic ceiling.

insights.claim: The Taliban are building an education system on the assumption that they will rule for generations, using it as the principal instrument to determine how Afghans think, whom they obey and what sort of state Afghanistan becomes.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Sets the planning horizon: policy toward Afghanistan should be modelled over decades of entrenched rule, not as a transitional phase.
insights.quote: It is an education system built by a regime that expects to rule for generations to come.
